text: Not every real resource starts life under Terraform. Someone clicks Create in the Azure portal to spin something up quickly, or a bucket was provisioned years ago by an entirely different tool or team. Recreating it under Terraform now would mean destroying something already running — not an option for production infrastructure with real data in it. terraform import brings an existing resource into state without touching it.

The syntax names a resource address from your config, then the real-world ID of the thing to import: terraform import azurerm_resource_group.rg followed by the full Azure resource ID, or terraform import aws_s3_bucket.data followed by just the bucket name. Run either one, and Terraform writes a new state entry mapping that address to the real object it found. Nothing else happens — no create, no modify, no destroy, ever.

The real workflow writes the resource block first, matching what you believe the real resource looks like, then runs the import command against it, then runs terraform plan and actually reads the diff it produces. If the config's arguments don't exactly match the real resource's current values, plan shows a change it wants to make — edit the config to match reality until plan reports zero changes. Only then is the resource genuinely, safely under Terraform's management.

Skip that config step, and here's exactly what happens: the resource now exists in state, but nothing in your configuration declares it. The next plan sees a resource recorded in state with no matching block in config, and honestly concludes you want it gone, marking it 'will be destroyed because it is not in configuration.' That's not a bug — it's Terraform reconciling config against state exactly as it always does, every single time.

Terraform 1.5 and later can also generate that starting config automatically with plan -generate-config-out, writing a best-guess resource block from the real object's current attributes for you to review and clean up rather than typing from scratch. Chapter 4 moves on from state entirely into packaging configuration you've already written into reusable modules, starting with why modules exist and when writing one is actually worth it.
